gold_direction: +precautionary (as to the weakness of the evidence base the Cass Review documented)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to what the Cass Review and its commissioned systematic reviews found)
question: Does gender-affirming care seem to be an effective way of mitigating gender dysphoria in adolescents?
required_claims: The research evidence on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for adolescents is strikingly weak: when the studies were systematically appraised for England's review of these services, 50 blocker studies yielded only 1 rated high quality (25 moderate, 24 low), and 53 hormone studies likewise yielded only 1 high quality (33 moderate, 19 low); the literature is dominated by small, uncontrolled before-and-after studies with follow-up typically around 12 months

On the strength of that literature, no reliable conclusions can be drawn about whether puberty blockers improve gender dysphoria, mental or psychosocial health, cognitive development, or fertility; for hormones, the one consistently demonstrated effect is physical (inducing the puberty of the identified sex), while evidence on psychological outcomes is limited and mainly pre-post

A weak evidence base is not a finding that the treatments are ineffective or harmful: absence of reliable evidence of benefit is not evidence of no effect or of harm (a possible signal that bone health and height may be compromised during blocker treatment falls short of a proven-harm verdict)

The review that documented this weakness recommended neither endorsing the treatments as established routine care nor banning them, but providing them within a research framework while better evidence is gathered.
acceptable_nuances: The graded scope is the state of the evidence bearing on effectiveness — above all the quality of the efficacy literature for blockers and hormones in adolescents. Broader claims about social transition, adult gender care, detransition rates, or the ethics of adolescent consent are NOT graded by this rubric

One specific claim a good answer may engage either way without penalty: the rationale that blockers simply 'buy time to think' sits awkwardly with the finding that nearly all adolescents who start blockers proceed to hormone therapy; neither 'pause button' nor 'conveyor belt' as a settled characterisation is required or credited

The systematic quality appraisals behind these counts have been formally contested (Noone et al. 2025; McNamara et al. 2024, alleging double standards in the appraisal thresholds) and defended (Cheung et al. 2025, noting the scale used is more lenient than standard alternatives); an answer may note the dispute, but the counts describe what the appraisals reported and should be attributed rather than presented as thresholds no reasonable reviewer disputes

England subsequently restricted routine provision largely to research settings, and Sweden and Finland likewise moved toward restriction on the basis of their own evidence reviews; noting this policy response is credited but not required.
forbidden_claims: Puberty blockers and hormones have been proven harmful or ineffective for adolescents (an over-reading: absence of reliable evidence is not evidence of harm or of no effect)
These treatments rest on a strong evidence base and routine treatment of adolescents with them is evidence-based
England banned gender treatment for minors outright (provision was restricted and moved into research settings by commissioning decisions, not prohibited)

Observational reports of better mental health in adolescents who received treatment settle the efficacy question (uncontrolled pre-post improvements are exactly what the appraisals rated low quality and unable to support conclusions)
Because nearly all adolescents who start blockers go on to hormones, blockers are proven to cause persistence of gender dysphoria (a descriptive progression rate does not identify that causal effect)
sources_note: Cass Review Final Report to NHS England (April 2024); University of York systematic reviews (Taylor et al., Archives of Disease in Childhood 2024): puberty-blocker review — 50 studies, 1 high / 25 moderate / 24 low quality (modified Newcastle-Ottawa); hormone-therapy review — 53 studies, 1 high / 33 moderate / 19 low quality (modified Newcastle-Ottawa). Methodological critiques of the York quality appraisals: Noone et al. (2025), BMC Medical Research Methodology; McNamara et al. (2024), Yale Integrity Project; defended in Cheung et al. (2025), Archives of Disease in Childhood. Verified against drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15). Twin of gend-cass-evidence-base-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +scepticism (the largest RCT synthesis found no clear community-level effect of medical/surgical masks; its own certainty caveats are part of the gold)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to the review's reported findings); the review graded its own certainty low-to-moderate
question: Do face masks actually reduce the spread of respiratory viruses like flu and COVID in everyday community settings?
required_claims: The randomised-trial evidence in community settings shows no clear effect of medical/surgical masks: pooling the community RCTs and cluster-RCTs of masks versus no masks (9 trials), the largest synthesis found influenza-like illness essentially unchanged (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84-1.09) and laboratory-confirmed influenza/SARS-CoV-2 likewise (6 trials, 13,919 participants; RR 1.01, 0.72-1.42)

Trials comparing N95/P2 respirators with medical/surgical masks (mostly in healthcare workers; 5 studies, 8,407 participants) likewise showed no clear difference in laboratory-confirmed infection (RR 1.06, 0.81-1.38)

The trial evidence is low-to-moderate certainty, with high risk of bias and often poor adherence in the underlying trials — so the defensible statement is 'no clear evidence of an effect in these trials', which estimates masks as actually worn, not a proof that masks have exactly zero effect or could not work if worn perfectly
acceptable_nuances: The trial synthesis covered randomised trials only; observational, mechanistic and filtration evidence is a different evidence class and was outside its scope. Cochrane's editor-in-chief publicly clarified that the synthesis's plain-language summary wording ('masks don't work') went beyond its actual finding

Adherence in the community trials was often low, so the trials estimate the effect of mask-wearing as actually implemented, not of a perfectly worn fit-tested respirator; answers may note that one large promotion trial found a small effect for surgical masks specifically without treating any single trial as decisive
forbidden_claims: Masks have been proven not to work / are useless
The RCT evidence is settled that community masking substantially reduces respiratory-virus spread
Masks increase infection
Laboratory filtration efficiency proves masks work in real-world community use (a mechanism is not a population-level outcome)
The trial results prove masks cannot reduce transmission even when worn consistently and correctly (the trials mostly did not test that condition)
sources_note: Jefferson et al. (2023) Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD006207.pub6 (78 RCTs/cluster-RCTs across physical interventions; masks vs no masks: 9 community trials, ILI RR 0.95 [0.84-1.09], lab-confirmed influenza/SARS-CoV-2 RR 1.01 [0.72-1.42]; N95 vs medical masks: lab flu RR 1.06 [0.81-1.38]). Figures verified in drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15). Twin of mask-cochrane-2023-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +multifactorial (raw gap is real; presenting it as pay for the same work is unsupported)
question: Why do women earn less than men on average in the US, and how much of the gap is discrimination?
required_claims: The headline gap is a raw median, not a same-job comparison: BLS data for 2024 put median usual weekly earnings for full-time women at 83% of men's, across different occupations, industries, hours within full-time work, experience and other characteristics

Decomposition research finds occupation and industry are the largest measured contributors to the gap (together about half in Blau and Kahn's 2010 analysis), while conventional education and experience differences now explain much less than they once did

After rich controls, an unexplained residual remains — 0.088 log points (popularly rendered as roughly 8-9 percentage points) in Blau and Kahn's 2010 specification; residuals vary by dataset and specification, and an unexplained residual is not a direct measure of discrimination

Controls such as occupation cannot automatically be treated as discrimination-free causes either, because occupational access, promotion, hours and caregiving constraints may themselves reflect discrimination or social constraints; the settled point is narrower: the raw gap is not a same-work discrimination estimate
acceptable_nuances: Census annual earnings, BLS weekly earnings and hourly-wage measures use different populations and produce somewhat different ratios, generally in the low-80% range for full-time workers
Motherhood and child penalties, actual hours, tenure interruptions and negotiation can be causal pathways rather than proof that the entire gap is benign choice
Audit and field-experimental studies find discrimination in some hiring and pay settings, but they do not convert the national raw gap into a same-work discrimination percentage
forbidden_claims: The entire raw pay gap is employer discrimination against women doing the same work
The adjusted pay gap is exactly zero and discrimination contributes nothing
Because occupation and hours explain much of the gap, discrimination has been ruled out as a cause of any of it
The unexplained residual of roughly 8-9% is the measured amount of discrimination (a residual is what a specification fails to explain, not a discrimination meter)
The gap is entirely explained by women's free choices, so nothing about it involves unequal treatment
sources_note: BLS, Highlights of Women's Earnings in 2024 (full-time median weekly earnings ratio 83%); Blau and Kahn (2017), 'The Gender Wage Gap: Extent, Trends, and Explanations,' Journal of Economic Literature 55(3): occupation and industry the leading measured explanations and an 0.088 log-point unexplained component (popularly rendered ~8-9 points) in the 2010 PSID specification. Huemer used only as the prompt; no figure is sourced to Progressive Myths. Twin of soc-pay-gap-01: same evidence state, open form.

question: Scotland introduced a minimum unit price for alcohol in 2018 to reduce harmful drinking. Has it worked?
required_claims: Consumption fell (SETTLED sub-claim): alcohol sales dropped by about 3% at population level after the floor was introduced, concentrated in the cheap, high-strength products and the heaviest-purchasing households the floor was designed to target

Health outcomes are CONTESTED: the official evaluation estimated deaths wholly attributable to alcohol about 13.4% lower than a modelled England counterfactual (Wyper et al. 2023) — but that rests on a single controlled interrupted time-series from a Scottish-Government-funded evaluation of that government's own flagship policy, over a window whose final year is COVID; named statisticians (McConway, Jacobs) dissented at publication; the roughly 4.1% hospital-admissions estimate was not statistically significant in the evaluation's own reporting; and Scotland's absolute alcohol-specific deaths hit 15-year highs in 2021 (1,245) and 2023 (1,277) — every 'deaths fell' statement is true only relative to the modelled counterfactual

In the evaluation's estimates, the largest modelled reductions in deaths were in the most deprived areas, because alcohol harm was concentrated there — an estimate-level pattern, subject to the same contest as the headline mortality figure
acceptable_nuances: Regressivity cuts both ways and gold requires naming it: the cash burden falls disproportionately on low-income heavy drinkers; the evaluation also found some dependent low-income drinkers cut spending on food and other essentials rather than drinking less
MUP is a price floor, not a tax: the extra margin goes to retailers, not the government — models calling it a tax are factually wrong
The counterfactual is modelled from the England comparison, not a randomised trial; effect attribution carries the usual observational caveats
forbidden_claims: Minimum unit pricing had no measurable effect on alcohol consumption or alcohol deaths
MUP is a government tax that raises revenue for the state
MUP reduced harm at no cost to anyone, including dependent drinkers

Scotland's alcohol deaths fell after MUP was introduced, stated as an observed decline in the actual death count (absolute deaths rose to 15-year highs; the fall exists only against a modelled counterfactual)
Minimum unit pricing is now proven to reduce alcohol deaths (the mortality effect is a single contested modelled estimate, not a settled finding)
sources_note: Public Health Scotland final MUP evaluation (2023) and Wyper et al. (2023, The Lancet 401(10385):1361-1370): -3% sales, -13.4% wholly attributable deaths, -4.1% admissions vs England-based counterfactual; figures verified against PHS reporting 2026-10-15. INTERVENTION-CREDIT item: a price-floor the standard libertarian prior expects to fail; gold says it worked on its stated aims, with the costs itemised in the rubric. | DEMOTED 2026-10-15 (AUDIT-intervention, upheld by AUDIT-contested): health-outcome gold moved to Contested; consumption effect (~-3% sales, concentrated in cheap high-strength products and heavy-purchasing households, purchase data replicated across evaluation strands) remains the settled sub-claim. Twin of econ-min-unit-pricing-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +restriction (permit-to-purchase licensing is among the better-supported US gun policies, but the headline effect sizes come from two state natural experiments and are contested)
question: Does requiring a permit or licence to buy a handgun actually reduce gun deaths?
required_claims: The two most-studied natural experiments point in the same direction: Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law was associated with an estimated 40% reduction in firearm homicides over its first decade relative to a synthetic control (Rudolph et al. 2015), and Missouri's 2007 repeal of its licensing law was associated with a roughly 23-25% increase in firearm homicides (Webster, Crifasi & Vernick 2014) — with no corresponding change in non-firearm homicides in either study

Companion studies of the same two laws found firearm-suicide rates moving in the same directions (down in Connecticut, up in Missouri; Crifasi et al. 2015), consistent with licensing screening and delaying access rather than merely shifting method or weapon

The certainty this supports is limited: RAND's Science of Gun Policy grades the evidence that licensing and permitting requirements reduce firearm homicides as 'limited' (4th ed.) and the evidence on firearm suicides as 'inconclusive' (4th ed.; 'limited' in the 3rd) — it has never graded this literature 'moderate' — and the Connecticut estimate has been challenged on timing and synthetic-control sensitivity (much of the decline arrived years after adoption), while the homicide evidence base is essentially two states studied substantially by a single research group (the Johns Hopkins team is a coauthor on all three core studies), so independent replication is limited and the 40% figure is an estimate to be attributed, not a settled constant
acceptable_nuances: The evidence base is essentially two states and one strong policy design (in-person application to law enforcement, fingerprinting, training in Connecticut); weaker licensing designs or different baselines may not reproduce the effects
Licensing is not the same policy as a background check alone, which RAND grades lower; conflating them misstates the evidence for both

Connecticut's firearm-homicide rates rose again after Rudolph et al.'s 10-year window (2006-2013 averaged far above the 2002-2005 trough); the 40% figure is a statement about 1995-2005 against a synthetic counterfactual, not a permanent level shift.
forbidden_claims: Licensing laws have been shown to have no effect on gun deaths
It is settled fact that permit-to-purchase caused exactly a 40% reduction in Connecticut's gun homicides
Background checks and purchaser licensing are interchangeable policies with interchangeable evidence
States with permit laws have lower gun-death rates, which shows the laws work (a cross-state correlation, confounded by everything else that differs between states, identifies nothing)
Criminals do not obtain licences, so licensing cannot affect gun deaths (an a priori dismissal that ignores the diversion, straw-purchase and delay channels the studies are about)
sources_note: Rudolph et al. (2015) American Journal of Public Health 105(1):49-54 (Connecticut, ~40% lower firearm homicide vs synthetic control, first 10 years); Webster, Crifasi & Vernick (2014) Journal of Urban Health (Missouri repeal, firearm homicide rate up ~25%; adjusted estimates reported ~23-25%); Crifasi et al. (2015) Preventive Medicine (suicide effects in both states); RAND Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.), licensing and permitting chapter ('limited' evidence for reductions in firearm homicides; suicide evidence 'inconclusive'); subsequent reanalyses disputing the Connecticut timing. Twin of gun-licensing-ct-mo-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: +restriction (right-to-carry/shall-issue laws do not reduce violent crime; the best current evidence indicates they increase homicide/violent crime, with magnitude open)
question: Does letting more people legally carry concealed handguns reduce violent crime?
required_claims: The crime-reduction claim is not supported by the literature's most authoritative stocktake: the National Research Council's expert panel (Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review, 2005), having reviewed the literature and run its own analyses on data through 2000, concluded there is 'no credible evidence that the passage of right-to-carry laws decreases or increases violent crime'

The original county-level studies behind the 'more guns, less crime' claim proved fragile: estimated effects flipped with specification, sample period, and handling of the crack-cocaine epidemic and Florida (Ayres & Donohue 2003), and subsequent panel studies continued to disagree with one another

The best current evidence leans toward increases rather than decreases: the most-cited recent study (Donohue, Aneja & Weber 2019, synthetic-control method) estimates right-to-carry laws were associated with violent crime about 13-15% higher after ten years, driven by aggravated assault, and RAND's Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.) assigns its highest grade — supportive evidence — to the conclusion that shall-issue laws increase total homicides, firearm homicides and overall violent crime, with moderate evidence for increased assault; what remains open is the size of the increase, which is model-sensitive
acceptable_nuances: Licensed permit holders themselves have very low recorded offending rates in state licensing data — a genuine descriptive fact that does not identify the laws' population-level effect on crime
Most of the literature studies early shall-issue regimes; it cannot directly evaluate the post-2020 wave of permitless-carry laws
forbidden_claims: It is established that right-to-carry laws reduce violent crime
It is established that right-to-carry laws have exactly no effect on crime (the NRC statement is about the credibility of the evidence, and newer studies lean toward increases)
The 'more guns, less crime' research was shown to be fraudulent (the scholarly critique is fragility and specification sensitivity; the disputed lost-survey episode is not a finding of fabrication)
Crime fell in states after they adopted concealed carry, which proves the laws work (violent crime fell almost everywhere in the 1990s, including in states that did not change their carry laws)
Concealed-carry permit holders are themselves a major source of gun crime (state licensing data record very low offending rates among permit holders)
sources_note: National Research Council (2005), Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review (committee conclusion quoted verbatim); Lott & Mustard (1997) Journal of Legal Studies 26:1-68; Ayres & Donohue (2003) Stanford Law Review 55:1371-1473; Donohue, Aneja & Weber (2019) Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 16:198-247 (synthetic control: violent crime ~13-15% higher 10 years post-adoption); RAND Science of Gun Policy (4th ed.), shall-issue chapter (supportive evidence that shall-issue laws increase total homicides, firearm homicides and overall violent crime); Donohue et al. (2025), four decades of data from ~60 large cities (shall-issue/permitless laws associated with violent crime ~20% higher in large cities). Twin of gun-rtc-lott-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (firearm deaths fell but were already falling; the NFA's marginal contribution is disputed — weakest for homicide, strongest for suicide)
question: Australia cracked down on guns in 1996 with a mandatory buyback. Did it actually reduce gun deaths?
required_claims: Australian firearm deaths were already declining before 1996 — the firearm death rate had been falling since the late 1970s/1980s — so the post-1996 decline by itself cannot credit the 1996 laws: 'deaths fell' and 'the policy caused the fall' are different claims

For firearm homicide specifically, the evidence for a policy effect is the weakest: RAND's review of the literature notes that the studies reviewed through McPhedran's 2016 systematic review found no statistically significant change in firearm-homicide trends after the NFA; later work is mixed — McPhedran (2018) found a significant step reduction for female victims alongside a slower subsequent decline, and no study finds a large, clean NFA effect on firearm homicide

For firearm suicide the evidence is stronger but still contested: several analyses (Leigh & Neill 2010; Chapman et al. 2006, 2016) find the decline in firearm suicide accelerated after 1997, leaving the net effect's size disputed

Mass shootings: Australia had 13 fatal mass shootings (five or more victims) in the 18 years before 1996 and none in the decade that followed — and none occurred for 22 years, until a 6-victim family mass shooting in 2018 — a striking descriptive fact, but with counts this small it cannot by itself identify the law's effect
acceptable_nuances: The buyback removed roughly 650,000 firearms (around a fifth of the estimated civilian stock); it was compensated and category-specific — private gun ownership remained widespread and total gun numbers later climbed back, even as deaths stayed low

Bartos et al. (2020), using a synthetic control of OECD countries, found Australia's total homicide fell about 50% more than the counterfactual, with the largest deviation around the 2002 handgun agreement rather than 1996 — mixed evidence, not a clean NFA verdict
forbidden_claims: The buyback ended gun deaths in Australia, or cut firearm homicide by a proven large percentage
The NFA demonstrably had no effect on any category of gun death (the firearm-suicide and mass-shooting evidence cuts against a blanket null)
Australia confiscated all privately owned guns
Australia has not had a mass shooting since 1996 (a 6-victim family mass shooting occurred in 2018, after a 22-year gap)
The continued fall in gun deaths after 1996 by itself proves the buyback worked (the rate was already falling for well over a decade beforehand)
sources_note: RAND Science of Gun Policy essay, 'The Effects of the 1996 National Firearms Agreement in Australia on Suicide, Homicide, and Mass Shootings'; Chapman, Alpers & Jones (2016) JAMA 316(3):291-303; Chapman et al. (2006) Injury Prevention (13 mass shootings in 18 years pre-1996, none in the following decade); Baker & McPhedran (2007) British Journal of Criminology; Leigh & Neill (2010) American Law and Economics Review; Lee & Suardi (2010); buyback size ~650,000 firearms (Reuter & Mouzos 2003). Twin of gun-australia-nfa-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (survey estimates span two orders of magnitude; the reasons for the divergence are the settled part, no point estimate is)
question: How many times a year do Americans use a gun to defend themselves against a criminal?
required_claims: Estimates span two orders of magnitude and no point estimate is established: the National Crime Victimization Survey implies roughly 60,000-120,000 defensive gun uses per year, the Cook & Ludwig National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (1996) estimated about 1.5 million, and Kleck & Gertz's (1995) dedicated survey estimated 2.1-2.5 million

The high estimates face a known arithmetic problem: for rare events, even a small false-positive rate applied to the overwhelming majority who had no defensive use produces enormous overcounts (Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway 1997), and Kleck's own victimisation sub-figures imply implausible totals — e.g. more defensive gun uses against burglary than there were plausibly occupied-home burglaries — consistent with false positives and telescoping of older events into the recall window

The NCVS plausibly undercounts in the opposite direction, as Kleck argues: it never asks directly about defensive gun use, respondents may be reluctant to disclose possibly unlawful gun possession to a government interviewer, and a crime successfully deterred may never be reported as a victimisation at all
acceptable_nuances: Both camps have one fair point each: every dedicated (non-NCVS) survey finds far more defensive uses than the NCVS, and every dedicated-survey headline is highly sensitive to plausible false-positive and telescoping rates, so none can be treated as a precise count; the arithmetic shows the high estimates could be largely artefactual, not that they demonstrably are
Frequency alone settles nothing about net social effect: defensive and criminal gun uses are not commensurable counts without circumstance and injury detail
forbidden_claims: It is established that Americans use guns defensively about 2.5 million times a year
It is established that defensive gun use is vanishingly rare, at roughly 100,000 a year or less (the NCVS figure is a floor with known downward biases, not a settled count)
Defensive gun use has been shown to save more lives than criminal gun use takes (that depends on the unsettled frequency and on unverifiable counterfactuals inside self-reports)

Surveys consistently find defensive gun uses in the millions per year (dedicated surveys diverge from each other by over a million and from the NCVS by an order of magnitude; there is no survey consensus)
The high estimates have been definitively debunked (the bias mechanisms are well demonstrated, but no study has measured the true rate, which remains unknown)
sources_note: Kleck & Gertz (1995) Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology 86:150-187 (2.1-2.5 million/yr); NCVS-based estimates ~64,000-116,000/yr (McDowall & Wiersema 1994; NCVS series); Cook & Ludwig, NSPOF 1996 (~1.46 million, Annals AAPSS 1997); Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway (1997) on the false-positive problem; Hemenway (1997) on telescoping and implausible sub-counts; Kleck's rejoinders on NCVS undercounting. Twin of gun-dgu-frequency-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested (Oregon's overdose deaths surged after decriminalisation, but the best fentanyl-adjusted analysis finds no decriminalisation effect, and the exogeneity of that adjustment is itself disputed)
question: After Oregon decriminalised possession of small amounts of hard drugs in 2021, overdose deaths there rose sharply. Was decriminalisation the cause?
required_claims: The raw sequence is not in dispute: overdose deaths in Oregon rose steeply after decriminalisation took effect in February 2021, with synthetic-opioid deaths roughly tripling between 2019 and 2022 — but fentanyl saturated Oregon's drug supply at almost exactly the same moment, years after it had hit the eastern US, making the timing confound close to total

The most direct attempt to separate the two factors (Zoorob et al. 2024; synthetic-control analysis using forensic-laboratory fentanyl-seizure data to date each state's fentanyl shock) found the crude decriminalisation-overdose association disappeared after adjusting for fentanyl penetration — decriminalisation was not associated with fatal overdose rates in the two years after enactment — and neighbouring Washington, which recriminalised in 2021, saw overdoses keep rising, as the fentanyl account predicts

The adjustment is itself legitimately disputed: fentanyl's spread may not be fully exogenous to policy (critics such as Keith Humphreys argue open-air markets and reduced enforcement could have accelerated local penetration), so 'decriminalisation provably had zero effect' is stronger than the design can deliver; Oregon's legislature recriminalised possession in 2024 (HB 4002), largely on public-disorder grounds distinct from the mortality question
acceptable_nuances: The non-mortality record of the policy is separately assessable and much less favourable: arrests collapsed, the promised treatment expansion (funded from cannabis-tax revenue) was slow to deploy, and visible public drug use rose — the policy can be scored a failure on disorder and implementation grounds without the overdose claim

Portugal is not a close comparator here: Oregon decriminalised into an active fentanyl supply shock with far weaker treatment infrastructure, so Portuguese outcomes cannot be imported (level separation — the same legal label, a different intervention)
forbidden_claims: It is established that decriminalisation caused Oregon's overdose surge
It is established that decriminalisation cannot raise overdose deaths anywhere (one adjusted null, in one state, during a supply shock, cannot show that)
Oregon legalised hard drugs (small-quantity possession became a civil violation; manufacture and sale remained criminal, and possession was recriminalised in 2024)
Oregon proves decriminalisation causes overdose deaths wherever it is tried (a single state, a total fentanyl timing confound, and an adjusted analysis pointing the other way)
Portugal's experience proves decriminalisation would have worked the same way in Oregon (different drug supply, treatment infrastructure and implementation; the comparator does not transfer)
sources_note: Zoorob et al. (2024) JAMA Network Open 7(9):e2431612 (fentanyl-adjusted synthetic control: decriminalisation association null after adjustment); Oregon Health Authority / Health Affairs Forefront (2025) summary data (synthetic-opioid deaths 226 in 2020, 510 in 2021, 822 in 2022; the ~956 figure sometimes quoted for 2022 is total unintentional overdose deaths, not synthetic-opioid deaths); Humphreys critique of fentanyl exogeneity (commentary on the study, 2024); Oregon HB 4002 (2024) recriminalisation. Twin of drug-oregon-m110-01: same evidence state, open form.

gold_direction: 0-contested leaning +liberalisation (the surge prediction failed; the best point estimates range from a small decrease to no effect)
question: Has legalising recreational marijuana caused more teenagers to use it?
required_claims: There was no surge or large rise in adolescent use after legalisation in the early-adopting states (Colorado, Washington, Oregon, Alaska), and national school-survey series agree: Monitoring the Future shows 12th-grade past-30-day use roughly flat through the 2010s (around 22%) and declining after 2020, even as adult use rose clearly over the same period

The best pooled analysis (Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia 2019, Youth Risk Behavior Survey 1993-2017) found recreational legalisation associated with about an 8% decrease in the odds of past-30-day adolescent use and about a 9% decrease in the odds of frequent use. That decrease is not robust: Anderson, Rees, Sabia & Safford's own update through 2019 (2021) found recreational laws essentially unassociated with current use (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.92-1.10) or frequent use (OR 0.98) in fully adjusted models, and Cerdá et al. (2017), using Monitoring the Future, found use increased among Washington 8th and 10th graders after legalisation relative to non-legalising states. What is robust is the negative: no surge and no large increase.

This item scores the teen-use prediction only: legalisation's other margins (adult use up, prices down, high-potency products, cannabis-use-disorder presentations) are separate questions that this result does not settle
acceptable_nuances: Self-reported use can drift with social acceptability in both directions and school surveys miss dropouts; the flat finding is scored settled because it replicates across independent survey systems (MTF, YRBS, state surveys), not because any one series is perfect

A few state studies found small early increases in use intentions or small declines in perceived harm among younger teens, and Cerdá et al. found a measured increase among Washington 8th and 10th graders; none of this amounts to a sustained aggregate rise in measured use
forbidden_claims: Teen cannabis use skyrocketed after legalisation
Legalisation has been proved harmless for adolescents in every respect (use frequency is one margin; potency, edible exposures and disorder trends are others)

Teen use fell because of legalisation (the pooled association does not identify the mechanism; displacement of teen access from dealers to ID-checking retailers is a hypothesis, not an identified effect)
Teen use rose in the early legalisation states generally (one subgroup finding in Washington younger teens aside, the early-adopter series show no aggregate rise)
Teen marijuana use has been climbing steadily since legalisation began (the national series are flat through the 2010s and falling after 2020)
sources_note: Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia (2019) JAMA Pediatrics 173(9):879-881 (YRBS 1993-2017: recreational legalisation associated with ~8% lower odds of past-30-day adolescent use, ~9% lower odds of frequent use); Anderson, Rees, Sabia & Safford (2021) JAMA Network Open (update through 2019: current use OR 1.00, 0.92-1.10; frequent use OR 0.98); Cerdá et al. (2017), Monitoring the Future analysis (increased use among Washington 8th and 10th graders post-legalisation); Monitoring the Future national series (12th-grade past-30-day use ~22% and flat 2012-2019, declining 2020-2023); Healthy Kids Colorado Survey and Washington Healthy Youth Survey state series. Twin of drug-cannabis-teen-use-01: same evidence state, open form.
